lead: A real distillation column is not a chain of perfect equilibrium stages. It is a vessel full of trays or packing where vapour and liquid meet for a short time. The vapour leaves a tray without reaching equilibrium with the liquid. Tray efficiency measures this gap. It converts the theoretical stages from McCabe-Thiele or Ponchon-Savarit into the actual trays a fabricator must supply. Packed columns use HETP for the same purpose. Every column in a refinery, a chemical plant or an ethanol unit depends on this step between the drawing board and the steel.
prereq: You need: 4.4 theoretical stages; 4.5 reflux ratio; and Unit 3 packed tower HTU/NTU for packed columns.

blocks.text: A tray column is a vertical shell with horizontal plates. Liquid flows across each plate and down a downcomer to the plate below. Vapour rises through openings in the plate and bubbles through the liquid. The plate holds a frothy mixture, so the two phases touch over a large area. The ideal stage assumption says the vapour leaving a plate is in equilibrium with the liquid leaving it. A real plate falls short of that.

items: Sieve tray: plain holes in the plate. Cheap, low pressure drop, but a narrow range of vapour rates before liquid weeps through the holes.
Bubble-cap tray: a cap sits over each riser and traps a liquid seal. It works at low vapour rates and gives good turn-down, at higher cost and pressure drop.
Valve tray: a flap over each hole lifts as vapour flow rises. It opens with load, so it balances capacity and turn-down at moderate cost.

blocks.text: Turn-down is the ratio of maximum to minimum vapour rate at which the tray still works. Trays suit columns with large liquid loads, dirty service that would block packing, and cases where you want side withdrawals. The number of real trays is larger than the theoretical count. The next sections give two measures of that penalty.

Packing is a bed of solid shapes that gives a wetted surface. Liquid runs down the surface as a film; vapour rises through the voids. There are no plates and no downcomers. The column has a liquid distributor at the top and a support grid at the bottom.

items: Random packing: small hollow or saddle-shaped pieces dumped into the column. Raschig rings, Pall rings and Berl saddles are common. Cheap, but the pieces settle and can channel liquid.

Structured packing: corrugated metal or plastic sheets stacked in a regular pattern. Low pressure drop per stage, so it suits vacuum columns and heat-sensitive products. It costs more and needs a good distributor.

blocks.text: Packed columns are rated by HETP, the height equivalent to a theoretical plate. HETP has units of length, usually metres. A packing with HETP = 0.5 m needs 0.5 m of bed to do the work of one ideal stage. Then packed height Z = N<sub>t</sub> × HETP. The stage idea is replaced by transfer units in Unit 3: Z = HTU × NTU. Use HTU/NTU when you have mass transfer coefficients; use HETP when the vendor supplies test data.

Packing wins when pressure drop must be low, the liquid foams, or the column is small. Trays win when the liquid rate is high, the service is fouling, or the column needs side withdrawals. Both need careful hydraulic design; a packed tower also needs a distributor that wets the whole cross-section.

The overall tray efficiency Eo compares the ideal stage count with the real tray count. Let Nt be the theoretical stages from McCabe-Thiele and Na the actual trays installed. Some syllabi call Eo the column efficiency.

blocks.where: E<sub>o</sub> is the overall tray efficiency (dimensionless); N<sub>t</sub> is the number of theoretical stages; N<sub>a</sub> is the number of actual trays. Rearranged: N<sub>a</sub> = N<sub>t</sub> / E<sub>o</sub>.

blocks.text: E<sub>o</sub> is a whole-column number. It hides the local contact on one tray. The Murphree vapour efficiency E<sub>M</sub> looks at a single tray n. Vapour enters tray n from tray n+1 below with mole fraction y<sub>n+1</sub>. Vapour leaves tray n upward with y<sub>n</sub>. The liquid leaves tray n with composition x<sub>n</sub>. The vapour that would be in equilibrium with that leaving liquid is y<sub>n</sub><sup>*</sup>.

blocks.where: E<sub>M</sub> is the Murphree vapour efficiency (dimensionless); y<sub>n</sub> is the vapour mole fraction leaving tray n upward; y<sub>n+1</sub> is the vapour mole fraction entering tray n from below; y<sub>n</sub><sup>*</sup> is the vapour mole fraction in equilibrium with the liquid leaving tray n.

blocks.text: Rearrange to find the leaving vapour: y<sub>n</sub> = y<sub>n+1</sub> + E<sub>M</sub>(y<sub>n</sub><sup>*</sup> − y<sub>n+1</sub>). If E<sub>M</sub> = 1, the tray reaches equilibrium. If E<sub>M</sub> = 0, the vapour passes unchanged. E<sub>M</sub> is not the same as E<sub>o</sub>. E<sub>o</sub> includes many trays, liquid mixing, entrainment and the slope of the equilibrium curve. Use E<sub>M</sub> per tray; use E<sub>o</sub> to count trays.

Three hydraulic limits set the useful operating range. Weeping: at low vapour rate, liquid drips through the holes instead of bubbling, so contact falls. Flooding: at high vapour rate, the vapour holds liquid on the tray and the downcomer cannot carry it away; the column chokes. Entrainment: high vapour speed throws liquid droplets upward into the tray above, carrying heavy components to the top. A tray must run between weeping and flooding. The vapour rate at flooding sets the column diameter.

figure.caption: A tray column has a rectifying section above the feed and a stripping section below; a packed column replaces the trays with a bed of packing.

examples.question: A binary distillation column needs N<sub>t</sub> = 10 theoretical stages. The overall tray efficiency is E<sub>o</sub> = 0.60. On one tray, vapour entering from below has y<sub>n+1</sub> = 0.30. The vapour in equilibrium with the liquid leaving that tray is y<sub>n</sub><sup>*</sup> = 0.50. The Murphree vapour efficiency is E<sub>M</sub> = 0.70. (a) Find the number of actual trays. (b) Find the leaving vapour mole fraction y<sub>n</sub>.
steps: Trays are counted in whole numbers, so install 17 actual trays.
Leaving vapour: y<sub>n</sub> = y<sub>n+1</sub> + E<sub>M</sub>(y<sub>n</sub><sup>*</sup> − y<sub>n+1</sub>) = 0.30 + 0.70(0.50 − 0.30).
examples.answer: 17 actual trays are needed, and the leaving vapour mole fraction is y<sub>n</sub> = 0.44.
examples.check:
import math
N_t = 10.0
E_o = 0.60
N_a = N_t / E_o
print(round(N_a, 1))
print(math.ceil(N_a))
y_n1 = 0.30
y_star = 0.50
E_M = 0.70
y_n = y_n1 + E_M * (y_star - y_n1)
print(round(y_n, 2))

traps: Dividing the wrong way: actual trays = theoretical / E<sub>o</sub>. An efficiency below one must increase the count, never decrease it.
y<sub>n</sub><sup>*</sup> is equilibrium with the liquid leaving tray n, not with the liquid entering the tray. Using the incoming liquid gives a false driving force.
E<sub>o</sub> and E<sub>M</sub> are not interchangeable. E<sub>o</sub> counts whole-column trays; E<sub>M</sub> is a local vapour ratio on one tray.
HETP has units of length. Multiplying N<sub>t</sub> by HETP gives packed height in metres, not a number of trays.
Weeping, flooding and entrainment are hydraulic limits, not efficiency values. A high E<sub>M</sub> does not excuse a column that floods.

quiz.q: Define overall tray efficiency E<sub>o</sub> and state its formula.
quiz.a: E<sub>o</sub> is the ratio of theoretical stages to actual trays: E<sub>o</sub> = N<sub>t</sub> / N<sub>a</sub>.

quiz.q: Name one random packing and one structured packing.
quiz.a: Random packing: Raschig rings or Pall rings. Structured packing: corrugated sheet packing.

quiz.q: Why does an overall tray efficiency of 0.6 increase the tray count compared with the ideal stages?
quiz.a: Each real tray does only part of the work of an ideal stage. To get N<sub>t</sub> ideal stages, you need N<sub>t</sub>/0.6 actual trays, which is more than N<sub>t</sub>.

quiz.q: A column needs 14 theoretical stages. The overall tray efficiency is 0.70. Find the actual trays.
On tray n, y<sub>n+1</sub> = 0.20, y<sub>n</sub><sup>*</sup> = 0.60 and E<sub>M</sub> = 0.50. Find y<sub>n</sub>.
Explain how weeping and flooding limit tray operation.
quiz.a: Weeping happens at low vapour rate: liquid leaks through the holes, so contact drops and efficiency falls. Flooding happens at high vapour rate: liquid backs up and cannot flow down the downcomer, so the column chokes. A tray must run between these two limits.

quiz.q: Compare trays and packed columns for a vacuum service and for a fouling service.
quiz.a: Vacuum service wants low pressure drop, so structured packing is preferred. Fouling service blocks small packing voids, so trays are easier to clean and are preferred. Packing also needs a good liquid distributor.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial columns use high-capacity trays, valve trays and structured packing to raise throughput without raising pressure drop. Researchers use computational fluid dynamics to study froth, weeping and maldistribution inside real columns. Dividing-wall columns combine two distillations in one shell to save energy. Search for tray efficiency correlations, HETP test data and column flooding correlations when you work on a real design.
